encyclopedia.summary: Machiko Hasegawa's four-panel comic about one Tokyo family. It began in 1946 and the TV anime that started in 1969 is recorded as the longest-running animated series in the world. The family's ordinary days are the entire content.
highlights: Nobody ages, which is how it has stayed on air for generations.
It is a decades-long record of how the Japanese family changed.
Conversation at the table matters more than plot — the template for everyday stories.

encyclopedia.summary: Osamu Akimoto's comic about the odd cops of one Tokyo police box. It ran from 1976 to 2016 and passed 200 volumes, and Guinness records it as the longest manga series by a single author. The characters' ridiculous habits matter more than the cases.
highlights: Repeating the same people and the same jokes for forty years became the form itself.
One small police box keeps showing a cross-section of Japanese society.
It is the clearest case of how a very long serial can keep going.

related.note: Another Japanese comic that ran for decades the same way
A work built on everyday places

encyclopedia.summary: Lucius, a bath-house designer in Rome, keeps slipping through time into modern Japanese baths and marvelling at the engineering. Mari Yamazaki's manga sets Roman and Japanese bathing culture beside each other and compares them through comedy. It was also made into a live-action film in 2012.

Modern Japan seen through a Roman's eyes is both strange and accurate.
Short episodes mean any volume can be read first.
